concept.name: Broker-dealer
concept.definition: A broker-dealer is a person or firm engaged in the business of both effecting securities transactions for the account of others (broker function) and buying and selling securities for its own account (dealer function). Under Section 15 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, most brokers and dealers must register with the SEC, join a self-regulatory organization such as FINRA, and become members of SIPC.
concept.intuition: A broker-dealer is the standard licensed securities firm: it can execute your trades as your agent and can also sell you securities out of its own inventory as principal.
concept.mechanics: The firm registers by filing Form BD through the CRD system operated by FINRA, obtains SEC registration and SRO membership, and must comply with net capital, books-and-records, supervision, suitability, and best-execution rules. Trade confirmations must disclose whether the firm acted as agent or principal and the compensation received.
concept.failure_modes: The dual agency/principal capacity creates conflicts of interest (e.g., selling from inventory, proprietary trading alongside customer flow) that disclosure mitigates but does not eliminate. Broker-dealer failure can transmit stress to clients and markets, as seen in 2008.
concept.misconceptions: A broker-dealer is not a fiduciary in all dealings by default — the historical standard was suitability/fair dealing, with Regulation Best Interest adding a best-interest obligation for retail recommendations. Registration does not mean the SEC has approved the firm's business or products.
concept.example: A full-service firm executes a customer's stock purchase as agent for a commission on one trade, and on another trade sells the customer a corporate bond from its own inventory as principal, disclosing its capacity on each confirmation.

citations.source: SEC, Division of Trading and Markets, Guide to Broker-Dealer Registration
citations.section: Parts II-III (registration; Form BD; SRO and SIPC membership)
